analysis.one_liner: Delays and weakens EPA's 2015 ozone smog standard and stretches health reviews from five years to ten.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced in February 2017, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, heard once at a subcommittee hearing in May 2017, and left to expire when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill pushes back the deadlines for states and the EPA to carry out the 2015 ozone (smog) standard by several years, changes the legal review cycle for air quality standards from five years to ten, and lets the EPA weigh technological feasibility — not just public health — when setting a standard. It also exempts the worst-polluting 'Extreme' ozone areas from required backup pollution measures, and blocks new smog limits from applying to permits for major industrial facilities until the EPA publishes implementing guidance. The 2015 ozone standard was already law; this bill would have slowed down and softened how it is put in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Power plants, factories, and other large emitters of ozone-forming pollution, which would have gotten years of additional delay before facing tighter smog limits and new permit requirements. State permitting agencies also get more time and, by statute, implementing guidance issued at the same time as any new standard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Power plants and large industrial polluters

how_it_helps.text: Delays the deadlines for states to designate areas under the 2015 ozone standard (to October 2024) and for the EPA to confirm those designations (to October 2025), with state implementation plans due by October 2026 — years later than the existing schedule.
Bars the EPA from completing or even proposing its next review of the ozone standard before October 2025, and stretches the review cycle for all health-based air standards from five years to ten.
Exempts ozone nonattainment areas classified as 'Extreme Areas' from the requirement to adopt contingency pollution-control measures.

Blocks the 2015 ozone standard from applying to preconstruction permits for major emitting facilities until the EPA publishes implementing regulations and guidance, and lets permit applications already in process proceed without the new standard.

analysis.who_pays: People who breathe the air — particularly children, older adults, and people with asthma — in areas that would remain out of compliance for longer, since the tightened smog limit would take years longer to reach and its next update could be delayed by up to a decade.
analysis.who_pays_short: People breathing smog, especially asthma sufferers

drawbacks.text: Every deadline in the bill is later than the existing Clean Air Act schedule, meaning more years before areas must actually cut the pollution that forms smog.
Changing the review cycle from five to ten years cuts in half how often the EPA must reexamine whether the smog standard protects health with an adequate margin of safety.
The bill writes 'technological feasibility' into the standard-setting process as a secondary consideration, moving away from the Clean Air Act's traditional health-only basis for the standard.
Exempting 'Extreme' ozone areas from contingency measures removes a safety net for the very regions with the worst smog.

The good-faith case for the bill: states and permit applicants argued the 2015 standard's timelines were unrealistic and that permitting uncertainty was stalling projects; the bill addresses that by giving states more time and requiring implementing guidance to be issued together with any new standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers states and industry real implementation relief — more time, clearer guidance, and fewer surprise permit rules. But the core of what it does is postpone, by years, the day when tighter smog limits actually clean the air, and it slows the machinery that updates health standards. The compliance savings for large emitters come directly out of additional years of smog exposure for the public, and the ten-year review cycle would leave an outdated standard in place for longer.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee after a single subcommittee hearing in May 2017 — no committee vote, no floor vote — and expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Capito introduced the bill on February 1, 2017, with six Senate cosponsors (six Republicans and one Democrat, Senator Manchin), and it was read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.
The committee's Clean Air and Nuclear Safety subcommittee held a hearing on the bill on May 23, 2017 — the only action the bill ever received.
No markup or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.
The 2015 ozone standard remained in effect, so the delays and exemptions in the bill never took force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who breathe the air are better off, because the multi-year delays and the exemption for the worst smog areas never became law and the 2015 standard's original schedule stood. Power plants and industrial emitters are worse off than they would have been under the bill, facing the existing deadlines for smog controls.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People exposed to smog, since the delays never passed

for.name: Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the Environment and Public Works Committee process.

for.name: Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining with fellow West Virginia senator Capito.

for.name: John Barrasso
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote on the bill; it advanced only to a subcommittee hearing in May 2017 and went no further.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican — six of the seven cosponsors were Republicans, with Senator Manchin of West Virginia the lone Democrat — and the bill never drew a floor vote, so no roll call exists.

industries.note: Coal- and gas-fired power plants are major sources of ozone-forming emissions and would have gotten years of delay before tighter smog limits and permit requirements took effect. The savings come from postponed pollution controls that would otherwise reduce smog-related illness.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and other large industrial facilities
industries.note: The bill blocks new smog limits from applying to preconstruction permits for major emitting facilities until implementing guidance is issued, sparing industrial projects from stricter air reviews. Ordinary people bear the cost as years of extra smog exposure.

States get several more years to submit designations and implementation plans, and new standards must ship with implementing guidance at the same time, easing their compliance workload — though the agencies' mission is protecting air quality, which the delays push back.
